# Characterizing Opsin Protein Spatial Expression and Ommatidia Morphology in *Speyeria mormonia* Butterflies: Insights into Function and Visual Ecology

### **By:** Sofia Diaz

 

## Introduction

The evolution of visual systems is central to evolutionary biology due to its contribution to species diversification. Investigations into color vision and visual systems have been instrumental in understanding how organisms perceive their environments and interact with one another (Gerl and Morris 2008). Unique visual genes, such as opsins, are responsible for detecting specific wavelengths of light and have been observed in various organisms (Terakita 2005). Located in retinal photoreceptor cells, opsins enable light detection, triggering phototransduction, which allows organisms to interpret visual cues (Briscoe and Chittka 2001). Studies have shown that gene duplications have led to the diversity of opsins, resulting in variation in photoreceptor types and visual abilities, and consequently, differences in behaviors in response to diversified opsin patterning across species (Briscoe and Chittka 2001; Frentiu et al. 2007; Feuda et al. 2016). Additionally, exploring the structure and morphology of the eye, such as ommatidia structure, provides a link to eye morphology and functionality. In butterflies, color vision is critical for behaviors like foraging, mate selection, and ovipositing (Arikawa 2017). Previous studies show that the compound eye of a butterfly is composed of many structural units called ommatidia with each individual ommatidium containing a cluster of nine photoreceptor cells, exhibiting opsin configurations that lead to species-specific visual abilities (Briscoe and Chittka 2001). Nymphalid butterflies are a diverse family of brush-footed butterflies that previous work has shown to possess limited photoreceptor diversity (McCulloch et al. 2016), typically displaying three to four spectral types of photoreceptors (McCulloch et al. 2016). The spatial expression of opsin proteins have been documented in some nymphalid butterfly species, highlighting opsin patterning of the R1 through R8 photoreceptor cells (McCulloch et al. 2016). To further understand the extent of photoreceptor diversity, color vision, and its link to function in Nymphalidae, additional nymphalid butterflies must be studied. In this project, I examined *Speyeria mormonia*, a nymphalid butterfly species from Colorado. *Speyeria mormonia* opsin expression has yet to be characterized at the protein level, and ommatidia morphology has yet to be documented. This study aims to characterize opsin protein expression and ommatidial morphology in male *Speyeria mormonia* butterfly eyes to explore opsin configurations and ommatidial structure in relation to their functions and visual ecology in their natural environment.

## Aims

My main goal in analyzing the *Speyeria mormonia* opsin expression and ommatidia morphology datasets was to compile initial data and figures to prepare for my dissertation research and identify key insights. To begin, I created two initial datasets from my larger *Speyeria mormonia* immunohistochemistry (IHC) dataset. The first dataset included the six highest-quality IHC images that showcased opsin expression patterning, specifically staining in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells. The second dataset consisted of five of the best longitudinal IHC images, highlighting the morphological structures of ommatidia from the eyes of five different *Speyeria mormonia* males. I aimed to visualize emerging patterns in both opsin expression and ommatidia morphology. Specifically, I wanted to assess the prevalence of different opsin patterns in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells and to determine the frequency of various ommatidia morphologies—such as whether the ommatidia exhibited straight or corkscrew configuration. This exploration process will inform the initial characterization of these features and guide my future research. Ultimately, I aimed to identify and quantify the patterns of opsin expression and ommatidia morphology in the eyes of male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies. Using tools like RStudio (Posit team, 2024\) to quantify and visualize these patterns, I sought to determine if consistent differences and similarities exist across male *Speyeria mormonia* eyes. The resulting pattern quantities will allow me to explore their functional and behavioral relevance, thereby deepening the understanding of color vision in the *Speyeria mormonia* system. 

## Data

During the summer, I conducted immunohistochemistry (IHC) experiments on male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies. I generated a large dataset of confocal images, examining the staining of the R1 and R2 photoreceptor cells to determine what opsin protein expression looked like in this system. The focal data I used for this proposal was ommatidia counts using these IHC images. Manual ommatidia counts were performed for the ommatidia opsin patterns of the R1 and R2 photoreceptor cells. Ommatidia subtypes were counted for six of the best-quality images, for morphology, five of the best-quality longitudinal section IHC images were used and individual ommatidia were marked based on morphological structure. Images were viewed at full resolution in ZEISS ZEN Lite (Carl Zeiss, 2026), and ommatidia were individually marked according to their R1/R2 photoreceptor cell staining. These eleven best IHC confocal images were used to establish a workable dataset to explore opsin patterning and ommatidia morphology.

## Methods

Ommatidia from the six best IHC images were manually counted, assessing both opsin expression and ommatidia morphology. All images were uploaded into Microsoft PowerPoint (Microsoft Corporation 2024\) and Zeiss Zen Lite (Carl Zeiss, 2026\) where individual ommatidia were counted and marked with color-coded outlined boxes that corresponded to opsin expression patterns defined by staining in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells. Only cells with clear, definitive staining in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells and slices where tissue was not folded, and cell bodies clearly labeled without high levels of background were included in the manual counts.

To generate the ommatidia morphology dataset, manual counts of ommatidia were performed. Only IHC images displaying clear, complete longitudinal ommatidia were included in the manual counting process. Each ommatidium was classified as either having a straight or corkscrew morphology, since these were the only two types observed in the IHC images. After both datasets were created, they were imported into RStudio (Posit team, 2024\) for visualization and plotting.                                                        

An exploratory analysis was conducted on the abundance and distribution of photoreceptor and ommatidia types to visualize the photoreceptor types and morphologies based on UV and blue expression, as well as straight versus corkscrew ommatidia found throughout the eye.

## Data Analysis

RStudio (Posit team, 2024\) was used to create stacked bar plots showing the relative abundance of both opsin expression patterns and ommatidia morphology types. These visualizations helped clarify the prevalence of each opsin expression pattern and ommatidia morphology present in the eyes of male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies.

Microscopy panel figures were created to clearly illustrate the different opsin expression patterns types—B-B, UV-UV, UV-B, and B-LW— found in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells of male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies. Additionally, a separate panel was created to depict the ommatidia morphologies, contrasting straight and corkscrew shapes to highlight the distinct ommatidia structures, making it easier to see both the characteristic opsin staining patterns and the structural differences between ommatidia types. The figures were prepared using Microsoft PowerPoint (Microsoft Corporation 2024\) and Zeiss Zen Lite (Carl Zeiss, 2026), which were used to showcase the configuration of images and presentation of both staining patterns in the photoreceptor cells and the structural features of the ommatidia.

## Results

The opsin expression pattern microscopy panel clearly displays the different opsin patterns—B-B, UV-UV, UV-B, and B-LW—defined by staining of the R1 and R2 photoreceptor cells. Sample GO35 was selected for this panel because it exhibited the clearest opsin signals in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells and was one of the samples with the most opsin expression pattern types within the dataset (Figure 3). The microscopy panel illustrating ommatidia morphology was created using sample G041, as this sample exhibited the most variety of both corkscrew-shaped and straight ommatidia (Figure 4). This allowed both ommatidia types to be shown together in the same panel, effectively highlighting their presence and variation within a single individual.

**Figure 3:** *Speyeria mormonia* male eye microscopy panel highlighting opsin expression pattern types. Images 1-4 show the R1-R8 photoreceptor cells mimicking the opsin expression patterns of the ommatidia selected from the IHC image.

 

 <img width="788" height="304" alt="Screenshot 2026-03-20 at 5 37 19 PM" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/33e4803a-61d9-4b10-90a9-fce9a019544c" />

**Figure 4:** Fluorescence microscopy panel of *Speyeria mormonia* male ommatidia morphology.  Showing the different examples of corkscrew morphologies seen in the ommatidia of males. Any ommatidia not showing this morphology was counted as straight.

The stacked barplot illustrating the relative abundance of opsin expression patterns displays the distribution of each opsin pattern type—B-B, B-LW, UV-B, UV-UV, and Dots—based on expression in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells of six male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies. Additionally, a distinct dot pattern was also observed going across the R1-R8 photoreceptor cells throughout the ommatidia in certain individuals. Each butterfly exhibited different numbers of ommatidia available for counting and showed a range of opsin expression pattern abundances. Specifically, samples GO27, GO35, GO37, and GO41 demonstrated at least four distinct opsin expression patterns in their R1/R2 photoreceptor cells (Figure 5). In contrast, samples GO40 and GO43 showed less variation, with GO43 containing only one opsin pattern and GO40 displaying up to three different opsin patterns in its R1/R2 photoreceptor cells (Figure 5).


<img width="698" height="431" alt="Screenshot 2026-03-17 at 6 37 39 PM" src="https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/bb1c9e72-cfa2-4328-b45b-520e075d0092" />

**Figure 5:** Relative abundance barplot for opsin pattern types characterized by opsin expression in the R1/R2 photoreceptor cells of six different *Speyeria mormonia* males.

The stacked barplot for ommatidia morphology types illustrates the variation in ommatidia morphology across five male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies. Among these, two individuals had only straight ommatidia, while the other three exhibited both corkscrew and straight morphologies. Sample GO37 had the lowest number of corkscrew-shaped ommatidia, whereas GO41 had the highest, followed by GO27, which had the second greatest abundance of corkscrew ommatidia (Figure 6). Samples GO26 and GO35 contained exclusively straight ommatidia, with no corkscrew types observed (Figure 6).

**Figure 6:** Relative Abundance barplot for ommatidia morphology types characterized by straight or corkscrew shaped ommatidia of five *Speyeria mormonia* males. 

## Discussion

The relative abundance barplots provided a clear visualization of the various opsin expression patterns found in each male *Speyeria mormonia* eye. These stacked barplots effectively highlight the diversity of both opsin expression patterns and ommatidia morphologies present. By using these visualizations, I can better interpret my opsin expression and ommatidia count datasets, which is essential for beginning to characterize the spatial distribution of opsin proteins and eye morphology in male *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies. As I proceed with ommatidia counts across my full dataset, I will be able to conduct statistical analyses to examine the variation and distribution of these pattern types in more detail. The dotted opsin pattern observed in some photoreceptor cells highlights a novel dot-stripped opsin pattern. This dotted pattern is specifically of interest as this opsin pattern type has been unique to that of male *Speyeria mormonia* male butterfly eyes. Further IHC experiments are required to quantify and better understand the extent of the dotted opsin expression pattern. Additionally, experiments on female *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies are needed to determine if this dotted pattern is sexually dimorphic. This will also allow me to test whether factors such as dorsal versus ventral eye regions are associated with specific opsin expression patterns or ommatidia morphologies. These figures and datasets form the basis of my analysis. As I collect more data and continue conducting ommatidia counts, I will create a comprehensive dataset for statistical analysis. This will allow me to analyze variations, identify significant patterns, and explore correlations between these patterns and factors such as eye region, sex, and eye depth, as well as opsin expression and ommatidia morphology. Ultimately, this research aims to connect these biological features to butterfly life history behaviors and function.

## Conclusion

By examining opsin protein expression and eye morphology, we can identify how species perceive color and their range of color vision. These insights will aid in understanding visual systems and their adaptations to various environments. The spatial expression of opsin proteins in *Speyeria mormonia* butterflies remains an unexplored frontier, representing a critical gap in our understanding of their visual system. By analyzing ommatidia structural types and opsin patterns, this research not only sheds light on the intricate mechanisms underpinning color vision in *Speyeria mormonia* but also highlights how unique cellular morphologies and protein expression drive distinct behavioral and ecological outcomes. This project aims to connect opsin expression and morphology with color vision, behavior, and ecological function in this butterfly species to gain a further understanding of the extent of color vision within the family Nymphalidae. Visualizing and characterizing these patterns will effectively communicate the spatial expression of opsins and the ommatidia data, offering valuable insights that could significantly advance our broader understanding of butterfly visual ecology and evolutionary biology.

## R code used for my Relative Abundance Plots

\`\`\`r

````shell
## ee282 Final Project Code ##
# Speyeria mormonia ommatidia counts and morphologies data 

setwd("/Users/sofiadiaz/Desktop/ee282_Coding_Course/")
```

```{r}
data <- read.csv("Speyeria_mormonia_ommatidia_counts.csv")
#data <- read.csv("Speyeria_mormonia_ommatidia_morph.csv")

head(data)
names(data)

library(ggplot2)
library(tidyr)
library(dplyr)

#starting with the Speyeria mormonia opsin pattern relative abundance plot
data_long <- pivot_longer(
  data,
  cols = -sample.ID,
  names_to = "OpsinPattern",
  values_to = "Count"
)

# Speyeria mormonia ommatidia count stacked barplot code: 

#stacked barplot shows the total amount of opsin patterns per individual butterfly

# run this before running any of the code for the barplots

library(RColorBrewer)

opsin_colors <- c(
  "UV.UV" = "#FF00FF", #magenta
  "B.B" = "#00008B",   #dark blue
  "B.LW" = "#008000", #dark green other codes #00CD00
  "UV.B" = "#800080", #purple
  "Dots" = "#FF8C00" #yellow #eede00 
)  

# Plot
ggplot(data_long, aes(x = sample.ID, y = Count, fill = OpsinPattern)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = opsin_colors) +  # Apply the custom colors
  labs(
    title = "Ommatidia opsin patterns in Speyeria mormonia",
    x = "Sample ID",
    y = "Number of ommatidia",
    fill = "Opsin pattern"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)  # rotate x labels for readability
)

# Adding the total opsin count per sample to the plot
totals <- data_long %>%
  group_by(sample.ID) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(Count))

# Plot
ggplot(data_long, aes(x = sample.ID, y = Count, fill = OpsinPattern)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = opsin_colors) +  

  geom_text(
    data = totals, 
    aes(x = sample.ID, y = total, label = total), 
    vjust = -0.5,  # slightly above the bar
    inherit.aes = FALSE,  # prevent conflicts with main aes()
    size = 2.5
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relative Abundance of Opsin Patterns",
    x = "Sample ID",
    y = "Number of Ommatidia",
    fill = "Opsin pattern"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.7) #to center the title
  )

#now working on the Ommatidia Morphology Relative Abundance Plots

data <- read.csv("Speyeria_mormonia_ommatidia_morph.csv")

head(data)
names(data)

data_long <- pivot_longer(
  data,
  cols = -sample.ID,
  names_to = "OmmatidiaMorphology",
  values_to = "Count"
)

library(RColorBrewer)

morphology_colors <- c(
  "corkscrew" = "#cc5500", #
  "straight" = "#008080"   #
)

# Ploting 
ggplot(data_long, aes(x = sample.ID, y = Count, fill = OmmatidiaMorphology)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = morphology_colors) +  # Apply the custom colors
  labs(
    title = "Relative Abundance of Ommatidia Morphology Types in Speyeria mormonia",
    x = "Sample ID",
    y = "Number of ommatidia",
    fill = "Ommatidia Morphology"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)  # rotate x labels for readability
)

# Adding the total ommatidia count per sample to the plot
#stacked relative abundance barplot

totals <- data_long %>%
  group_by(sample.ID) %>%
  summarise(total = sum(Count))

# Plot
ggplot(data_long, aes(x = sample.ID, y = Count, fill = OmmatidiaMorphology)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity") +
  theme_classic() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = morphology_colors) +  

  geom_text(
    data = totals, 
    aes(x = sample.ID, y = total, label = total), 
    vjust = -0.5,  # slightly above the bar
    inherit.aes = FALSE,  # prevent conflicts with main aes()
    size = 3
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Relative Abundance of Ommatidia Morphology Types",
    x = "Sample ID",
    y = "Number of Ommatidia",
    fill = "Ommatidia Morphology"
  ) +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 0.7),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.9) #to center the title
  )
````
